strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: moving mobile GUI agents from passive instruction following toward proactive intent suggestion and personalized execution.

FingerTip 20K appears meaningfully different from prior mobile-agent datasets by collecting longitudinal real-device interactions, user context, historical intents/actions, screenshots, accessibility trees, and action traces from 95 users over about one month.

The benchmark defines two concrete tracks and evaluates a broad set of generalist VLMs and GUI-specialized agents, plus fine-tuned variants, giving a useful first picture of current model limitations.

The paper includes several helpful supplementary analyses, including out-of-domain subsets, ablations over context/history/screenshots, joint vs separate fine-tuning, and a user study relating the personalization metric to subjective ratings.
The motivation is timely and the dataset, if released with strong privacy protections, could be valuable infrastructure for studying personalized mobile agents.
weaknesses: The proactive task suggestion formulation is arguably ill-posed: predicting a user's exact current intent from profile, time, location category, and history is inherently ambiguous, and even human annotators reach only 30.3% success. This weakens the interpretation of low model scores as a model capability gap rather than task ambiguity.

The evaluation metrics are not sufficiently validated. SR1 relies on DeepSeek-V3 as an automatic judge, while Sim1 mixes sentence embeddings and Levenshtein similarity in a way that may not reflect semantic correctness. For personalized execution, Sim2 is based on Levenshtein similarity over action strings normalized by a 'different type' user trace, which is a fragile proxy for personalization.

The personalization analysis is shallow: user 'type' is mainly age-group based, and it is unclear whether observed action-sequence differences reflect genuine preferences, app/UI state differences, device differences, or task/content differences.

Train/test splitting preserves substantial user overlap and temporally adjacent behavior, so fine-tuning gains may partly reflect memorization of users, apps, or repeated habitual intents. The out-of-domain tests are small and do not fully resolve this concern.

Privacy and ethics remain a major concern. The dataset contains real screenshots, accessibility trees, user profiles, timestamps, locations, app usage, and even an 'address' profile field. The mitigation strategy of instructing users not to upload private data plus manual/ML screening of first and last screenshots is unlikely to remove sensitive information reliably from full UI traces.

Reproducibility is under-specified despite the claim of open resources: anonymous links are blank in the manuscript, and details about live app environments, manual success checking protocol, annotator agreement, and exact evaluation infrastructure are insufficient.

The personalized execution success rates of the fine-tuned model remain far below the best GUI-control baseline, so the claim that the approach builds stronger personalized agents is only partially supported: it improves the proposed similarity metric but not robust task completion.

The paper would benefit from stronger baselines, such as retrieval/habit-frequency baselines for proactive suggestion, nearest-history imitation baselines for personalization, and privacy-preserving or redacted-data variants.

strengths: The paper identifies a timely and underexplored problem: mobile GUI agents that proactively infer user intent and personalize execution rather than merely following explicit instructions.

The proposed data collection has some appealing properties relative to prior Android benchmarks, including longitudinal traces, user profiles, time/location context, historical intents/actions, and real-device interaction across many apps.

The paper evaluates a reasonably broad set of generalist VLMs, GUI-control models, and prompt-based agents, and includes useful supplemental analyses on screenshots, historical intents, contextual fields, out-of-domain subsets, and the Sim2 metric.
The writing is generally understandable, and the benchmark framing is easy to follow.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is weakly supported. Proactive task suggestion is evaluated largely by sentence similarity and an LLM judge against a single recorded intent, but many proactive suggestions can be valid even if they differ from the logged next action. Conversely, high textual similarity does not necessarily imply useful or acceptable proactive assistance.

The personalization metric Sim2 is not convincing as a main claim. It is based on Levenshtein similarity over action strings relative to another user type, which may confound UI state, app behavior, task success, and sequence length with genuine user preference. The small user-rating validation only covers four models and does not establish robust metric validity.

The benchmark design risks leakage and shortcut learning. The test sets are sampled from later data for the same users, and historical intents/actions may include highly repetitive tasks. The paper argues this is intended, but it makes it hard to separate personalization from memorization or temporal frequency prediction. The OOD tests are small and not sufficient to resolve this.

Reproducibility and release details are inadequate. The manuscript repeatedly claims code/data are open-source, but the anonymous link appears blank in the PDF text and no accessible resource is provided. The dataset also depends on real Chinese apps and physical devices, making independent reproduction of execution results difficult.

The ethical and privacy treatment is insufficient for the sensitivity of continuous mobile screenshots, accessibility trees, locations, timestamps, user profiles, and personal action traces. Asking participants not to upload private data plus manual/ML inspection is not enough; residual re-identification and sensitive-behavior leakage remain major concerns, especially if the data are released.

The data population is narrow: 95 users, all in mainland China, mostly Chinese apps, with an average age of 25.9. This is acknowledged, but the paper still makes broad claims about mobile agents and personalization without strong evidence of generality.

The fine-tuning results are not as strong as the paper suggests. For personalized execution, the fine-tuned model improves Sim2 but has much lower task success than UI-TARS, so the claimed progress toward practical personalized agents is limited.

Several experimental choices are under-specified or fragile, including manual success checking for SR2, use of DeepSeek-V3 as both category/metric annotator, prompt adaptations for different GUI agents, and the exact data filtering/quality-control process. These details matter greatly for benchmark credibility.

Overall, the benchmark idea has promise, but the current paper does not provide sufficiently sound metrics, privacy safeguards, reproducibility, or evidence of generalizable impact for acceptance at a top-tier AI venue.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and underexplored problem: moving mobile GUI agents beyond passive instruction following toward proactive intent suggestion and personalized execution. This is a meaningful direction for user-facing agents.

FingerTip 20K appears to be a valuable dataset contribution: 21,437 longitudinal Android interaction episodes from 95 real users, across 506 apps, with intents, screenshots, accessibility trees, actions, timestamps, scenario labels, and user profiles. The real-device, daily-use collection setting is a major strength compared with simulator- or annotator-driven datasets.

The two benchmark tracks are clearly motivated and distinct: predicting latent user intent from context/history, and executing known tasks while matching user-specific action preferences. This gives the benchmark a concrete identity rather than being just another GUI-control dataset.

The paper evaluates a broad set of models, including generalist MLLMs, GUI-specific agents, prompt-based agents, and fine-tuned Qwen-2.5-VL variants. The results show large gaps in current models and demonstrate that training on the proposed data improves proactive and personalized behavior.

The appendices add useful ablations and analyses, including out-of-domain tests, the effect of screenshots/history/contextual fields, joint versus separate fine-tuning, and a small user study correlating the personalization metric with subjective ratings.

The authors acknowledge privacy issues and describe consent-like active data collection, user deletion ability, manual filtering, and model-assisted privacy screening, which is important for this type of dataset.
weaknesses: The evaluation metrics are a central weakness. Proactive intent success is judged by DeepSeek-V3, and personalization relies heavily on Levenshtein similarity over action strings normalized against a different-user sequence. These proxies are plausible but not fully validated, and they may reward surface similarity rather than genuinely useful or acceptable agent behavior.

The proactive task formulation may be intrinsically ambiguous: without screenshots, even humans achieve only 30.3% success. This raises questions about whether single-intent prediction is the right target, whether multiple acceptable intents should be modeled, and how much low success reflects benchmark difficulty versus label uncertainty.

The privacy and ethics discussion is not yet sufficient for a top-tier benchmark involving real personal phone use. User profiles include sensitive attributes and location-like scenario information; screenshots and accessibility trees may expose private data. The paper should more clearly specify consent, anonymization, release filtering, residual leakage risk, and whether raw screenshots/XML will be public.

The dataset is geographically and linguistically narrow, apparently centered on Chinese apps, Chinese prompts/intents, and a single regional ecosystem. This is acceptable as a first benchmark, but the paper’s broader claims about mobile agents and user-oriented behavior should be more carefully bounded.

The personalized execution track has a tension between task success and personalization: the fine-tuned model improves Sim2 but has much lower SR2 than UI-TARS. It is not fully clear that higher Sim2 translates into better practical agents when completion accuracy remains poor.

Some experimental details remain underspecified or hard to audit, including exact data release contents, human annotation protocol for SR2, DeepSeek judging prompts/calibration, participant recruitment details, and whether the same users/tasks create leakage through repeated habits across train/test despite temporal splitting.

The novelty is strongest as a dataset/benchmark contribution rather than a modeling contribution. The fine-tuning results are useful but methodologically straightforward, so acceptance depends heavily on the dataset’s quality, availability, and ethical robustness.
